props.title: Detective Conan: The Time Bombed Skyscraper
props.initialSlug: Teen detective races to stop tower bomb plot

sections.content: **Detective Conan: The Time Bombed Skyscraper** (1997) launched the theatrical film series of Japan's beloved detective franchise with explosive style. Building on the success of **Case Closed/Detective Conan** (1996- ) anime series, this feature film amplifies the core elements that make Conan compelling - intricate mysteries, ticking-clock tension, and the unique premise of a brilliant detective trapped in a child's body. The film's towering urban setting and bomb threat scenario drew clear inspiration from **Die Hard** (1988) and **Speed** (1994), while maintaining the distinctly Japanese approach to mystery storytelling seen in films like **The Castle of Cagliostro** (1979).

sections.content: The film established the winning formula that would define the Detective Conan movie series - taking the intricate mystery-solving of the TV episodes and expanding it to cinematic scale. Like **The Castle of Cagliostro** (1979) did for Lupin III, Time Bombed Skyscraper proved that Detective Conan's formula could work brilliantly in feature length. The film's success paved the way for what would become one of anime's longest-running and most successful theatrical franchises, with each subsequent film raising the stakes while maintaining the core appeal of watching a child-sized genius outsmart dangerous criminals.

Director Kenji Kodama, who helmed many of the TV episodes, brings theatrical flair while staying true to the source material's intricate mystery roots. The influence of classic detective films like **Sleuth** (1972) and **Murder by Death** (1976) shows in the careful plotting and misdirection, while the modern urban setting and action sequences draw from contemporary thriller conventions established by films like **The Fugitive** (1993). sections.content: The film's success helped establish a template for anime detective stories that influenced later works like **Detective School Q** (2003) and **Beautiful Bones: Sakurako's Investigation** (2015). The blend of intricate mystery plotting with high-stakes action sequences created a distinctly Japanese approach to the detective genre, different from Western procedurals like **Sherlock Holmes** (2009) or **Knives Out** (2019).
